question: How is LLM inference computed and searched efficiently: prefill/decode, decoding algorithms, serving-efficiency techniques, and inference-time scaling?
contributions: Decoding algorithms: greedy, beam, top-k, top-p, temperature, penalties, speculative decoding, stopping
Serving techniques: prefix caching, batching, continuous batching, PagedAttention, chunked prefilling, parallelization
Inference-time scaling: context, search, ensembling, verifiers, long thinking, training-based

results.claim: Beam widths of 2 to 5 are usually sufficient for high-quality generation; gains diminish with larger beams.
results.setup: Beam search in practical LLM inference
results.quote: In practical LLM inference, a relatively small beam width, such as K = 2 to K = 5, is usually sufficient to achieve high-quality generation.

results.claim: Self-attention for one generated token costs 2i' vector products, so generating len tokens is quadratic in length.
results.setup: Standard Transformer decoder, L layers, hidden d, KV cache not reducing attention reads
results.quote: Hence, generating a sequence of length len has a time complexity of O(L×d×len2) for the self-attention

results.claim: Top-p worked example in Fig 5.5(d): with p=0.6 only two tokens (renormalised .51/.49) remain.
results.quote: select top-ranked hypotheses whose probability sum ≥p = 0.6,

results.claim: Top-k worked example in Fig 5.5(c): k=3 renormalises .34/.32/.21 to .39/.36/.25.
Top-p with p=1 and temperature approaching zero is equivalent to greedy search.
results.quote: if we set p to 1 and β to a very small number (approaching zero), the top-p sampling method will become equivalent to the greedy search method.

results.claim: Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023) accepts a draft token if q<=p, else rejects with probability 1-p/q; the example uses tau=5 draft tokens.
results.setup: Draft model Pr_q, verifier Pr_p; greedy variant described; Fig 5.7 uses tau = 5
results.quote: (a) Predict the next τ tokens given the context using the draft model (τ = 5)

results.claim: Prefilling is compute-bound, decoding is memory-bound (Table 5.1).
results.quote: the prefilling process is considered compute-bound.

results.claim: Continuous batching has n+1 iterations for a sequence: one prefill and n decode steps; it is prefill-prioritised, raising throughput at the cost of latency.
results.quote: there are n + 1 iterations in total: one for prefilling, and n for generating the output tokens (one per token).

results.claim: Chunked prefilling lets a 3-chunk prefill overlap three decode steps instead of one.
results.quote: we can perform three decoding steps, rather than only a single decoding step

results.claim: No empirical benchmark numbers (speedups, accuracies) are given in the chapter.
results.quote: Inference is now a wide-ranging topic that encompasses many techniques.

limits: Textbook chapter: no experiments, speedups or throughput numbers; all quantitative content is illustrative (Fig 5.5 probabilities, tau=5).
Serving is explicitly left shallow: 'Here, we will not go into the details of LLM serving.'
Quantization, pruning, distillation and long-context attention are deferred to earlier chapters (2, 3, 4); KV-cache memory size formulas, GQA/MLA, FlashAttention are not given.
Tied to 2025 view (o1, R1, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI); serving landscape moves fast.
PDF has no reference list, so citations (Fan 2018, Holtzman 2020, Kwon 2023...) can't be resolved to titles from this file.
Speculative decoding is described only in its greedy version ('For simplicity, we describe the greedy version').
practices: Use greedy or beam search when deterministic, predictable output is needed (formal documents); use sampling for creative/open-ended generation (5.1.3.3).
Keep beam width small, K=2 to 5 (5.1.3.2).
Tune k or p carefully: too small is near-greedy, too large gives degenerate output (5.1.3.3).
Lower temperature sharpens the distribution, higher flattens it (5.1.3.3).
Pick a draft model that trades cost against acceptance length n_a (5.1.3.5).
Stop on EOS, max length, time budget, low token probability, or repetition detection (5.1.3.6).
Report quality and efficiency metrics together: latency, throughput, TTFT, ITL, utilisation, energy, cost (5.1.4).
Cache KV states of common prefixes keyed by hash of prefix tokens, with LRU eviction (5.2.1).
Bucket requests by length to cut padding in batches (5.2.2).
Use continuous (iteration-level) batching for throughput; use chunked prefilling to bound decode latency (5.2.2.2, 5.2.2.4).
Use PagedAttention-style fixed-size KV blocks to avoid fragmentation (5.2.2.3).
Disaggregate prefill and decode only with a high-bandwidth, low-latency network for KV transfer (5.2.2).
Choose verifiers by availability: tools/tests, trained reward model, LLM judge, majority vote (5.3.4.1).
Prefer diverse ensemble members; gains diminish with more members (5.3.3).
